revision_notes: Original score 0 with DataReportal cited was correctly flagged: DataReportal reports mobile connections (19.9m, 92.1% of population in 2025), not unique subscribers. Checked ITU/World Bank SIM-based mobile-cellular subscriptions (108.71 per 100 people, 2024) and ZICTA regulator data (99% subscription rate, 2022, via a Londa digital-rights report) — both are SIM/connection-based and inflated by multi-SIM ownership, so not usable for the 'unique subscriber' scale. Zambia's 2022 census records 40.8% of the population owning 'ICT devices' generally (broader than mobile phones specifically). GSMA has published a dedicated Zambia country report (Oct 2024) and a Zambia-specific chapter in its Nov 2025 'Accelerating Smartphone Adoption in Africa' report, either of which likely contains the precise unique-subscriber percentage, but this figure could not be extracted with the tools available in this session. No authoritative unique-subscriber percentage was confirmed; kept at 0/Unknown and flagged for a human with full GSMA Intelligence access to resolve.
revised_comments: Authoritative unique mobile subscriber penetration data for Zambia (as distinct from SIM or connection counts, which are inflated by widespread multi-SIM ownership) is not confirmed from publicly accessible GSMA or ITU sources.

Definition: The proportion of the population with basic digital skills (ability to use a computer, smartphone, or the internet for simple tasks such as sending messages, finding information, or using apps). Based on ITU household survey data, Afrobarometer, or national ICT surveys.
Comments: No Zambia-specific % with basic digital skills found in authoritative source within time; Afrobarometer policy paper provides multi-country methodology but not Zambia figure extracted here.
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: The originally cited Afrobarometer paper was a cross-country methodology piece with no Zambia-specific figure, correctly flagged. Found two Zambia-specific candidate figures mapping to different scale bands: (1) Zambia's 2018 ZICTA National ICT Survey found only 6.8% of individuals reported having 'adequate skills to use a computer' — still cited as the baseline in the government's 2023 National ICT Policy — which would fall in band 1 (<10%); (2) Zambia's 2022 Population and Housing Census (published 2025) found internet usage of 15% of the population aged 5+, which would fall in band 2 (10-24%). These measure different things (narrow computer literacy vs. broader internet use) and are of different vintages. No single ITU household ICT-skills aggregate specific to Zambia could be retrieved (the relevant 2025 ITU/Zambia ICT survey document was inaccessible). Given the ambiguity between bands 1 and 2 depending on which proxy is used, this is flagged for human review rather than asserting either code.
revised_comments: Estimates of basic digital skills in Zambia vary depending on definition: Zambia's 2018 national ICT survey found only 6.8 percent of individuals reported adequate computer skills, while the 2022 national census found 15 percent internet usage among the population aged five and above. Both figures point to still-low but rising levels of basic digital skill and use.

Definition: The gap between men and women in mobile internet usage or internet access. Based on the GSMA Mobile Gender Gap data or ITU gender-disaggregated ICT statistics. A smaller gap indicates more equitable access to digital opportunities.
Comments: No GSMA Mobile Gender Gap indicator for Zambia retrieved in this run; available gender/ICT report exists but not GSMA metric required.
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: The originally cited World Bank report addressed gender and ICT gaps in Zambia generally but did not map to the required GSMA/ITU gender-gap metric, correctly flagged. Zambia is not among the roughly 15 countries surveyed in GSMA's Mobile Gender Gap Report series, so no current GSMA country-level figure exists. The best available Zambia-specific data is the 2018 ZICTA National ICT Survey, as reported in Paradigm Initiative's Londa 2022 Digital Rights and Inclusion in Africa report: internet access stood at 17% for males vs. 12% for females, a relative gap of roughly 29%, which falls in the 'Moderate gap (20-29%)' band. Separately, GSMA's Mobile Connectivity Index case study on Zambia reports the gender gap in mobile phone ownership (a narrower, different measure) fell from 13% (2015) to 6% (2021). Given the variable specifically targets the internet usage/access gap, the ZICTA/Londa figure is used, though it rests on a single dated source (2018) and no more recent country-specific figure could be found; flagged for human review rather than asserted with confidence.
revised_comments: Zambia's most recent country-specific gender-disaggregated ICT data (the 2018 national ICT survey) shows a moderate gender gap in internet access, with 17 percent of men compared with 12 percent of women reporting internet use — a relative gap of around 29 percent. By contrast, the gap in basic mobile phone ownership is narrower, having fallen from 13 percent in 2015 to 6 percent in 2021, while smartphone ownership shows near gender parity.
